Learning with Locally Private Examples by
Inverse Weierstrass Private Stochastic Gradient Descent

Jean Dufraiche Affiliation: Univ. Lille, Inria, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189 - CRIStAL, F-59000 Lille, France Correspondence to: jean.dufraiche@inria.fr    Paul Mangold Affiliation: CMAP, CNRS, École polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91120 Palaiseau, France    Michael Perrot Affiliation: Univ. Lille, Inria, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189 - CRIStAL, F-59000 Lille, France    Marc Tommasi Affiliation: Univ. Lille, Inria, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189 - CRIStAL, F-59000 Lille, France
Abstract

Releasing data once and for all under noninteractive Local Differential Privacy (LDP) enables complete data reusability, but the resulting noise may create bias in subsequent analyses. In this work, we leverage the Weierstrass transform to characterize this bias in binary classification. We prove that inverting this transform leads to a bias-correction method to compute unbiased estimates of nonlinear functions on examples released under LDP. We then build a novel stochastic gradient descent algorithm called Inverse Weierstrass Private SGD (IWP-SGD). It converges to the true population risk minimizer at a rate of 𝒪⁡(1/n)\mathcal{O}(1/n), with nn the number of examples. We empirically validate IWP-SGD on binary classification tasks using synthetic and real-world datasets.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Machine Learning (ML) models are increasingly deployed in domains involving sensitive data, such as healthcare, speech recognition, prediction, and forecasting. These models are vulnerable to inference attacks that allow adversaries to extract information about individual training examples (Hu et al., 2022). This has motivated the use of Differential Privacy (DP) (Dwork & Roth, 2014) as a rigorous standard to assess privacy in ML. To achieve meaningful guarantees, DP typically requires data to be centralized by a trusted curator, in charge of enforcing privacy. Unfortunately, this raises several risks: the trusted authority may fall victim to attacks that lead to major data breaches (Primoff & Kess, 2017; Lu, 2019), and data may be misappropriated by untrustworthy third parties that do not prioritize privacy.

Local Differential Privacy (LDP) (Kasiviswanathan et al., 2008; Duchi et al., 2018) addresses this challenge by requiring each data holder to privatize their data locally before release, effectively ensuring privacy without relying on a trusted curator. While this provides strong privacy guarantees, applying it in ML requires adapting the downstream learning process. Existing methods can be categorized into interactive and noninteractive approaches. In interactive methods, the learner adaptively queries data holders over multiple rounds, incurring a communication cost (Smith et al., 2017). In contrast, noninteractive methods require each user to release one or several privatized versions of their data in a single shot, eliminating the need for further interaction during learning (Zheng et al., 2017).

In practice, designing LDP mechanisms involves two considerations: whether downstream learning tasks are known, and whether data release can be adapted during learning. In some scenarios, the downstream learning problem is known, and task-specific algorithms can be designed to correct for LDP noise; however, this limits the potential for the data to be reused for other purposes. In contrast, many real-world scenarios involve unknown downstream tasks or require that data remain reusable in the long run. This motivates the use of task-agnostic, noninteractive LDP methods.

In task-agnostic LDP, each data holder publishes a one-time privatized representation of their data, without prior knowledge of the downstream learning task. Such a mechanism allows institutions or users to safely publish privatized datasets that remain usable for future analyses, for example, hospitals sharing medical records for research purposes. Yet, despite its generality, noninteractive and task-agnostic LDP raises a significant challenge. Indeed, learning from noisy (private) data may bias the process, as previously identified in supervised learning with noisy features (Bishop, 1995) and labels (van Rooyen & Williamson, 2018). Naively applying standard ML frameworks to privatized data may yield suboptimal models: new algorithms tailored for noninteractive and task-agnostic LDP are thus needed.

Contributions.

In this paper, we develop a principled view of learning under noninteractive and task-agnostic LDP, and design new algorithms for locally private ML. We show that standard LDP mechanisms can be viewed, in expectation, as functional transforms: the Gaussian mechanism corresponds to the Weierstrass transform, while Randomized Response induces what we call the Bernoulli transform. This perspective allows us to fully characterize the bias induced by LDP on data-dependent computations.

Crucially, inverting these transforms allows the design of algorithms that provably mitigate privacy-induced bias, yielding unbiased estimators for the underlying data-dependent quantities. In learning contexts, we leverage the inverse of these transforms to construct unbiased gradient estimators for loss functions. Applying this principle to first-order optimization, we introduce Inverse Weierstrass Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (IWP-SGD). We show that IWP-SGD asymptotically recovers, in expectation over the noise, the population risk minimizer of the original, non-private problem, as the number of samples nn grows to infinity. Interestingly, the convergence rate of IWP-SGD scales as 𝒪⁡(1/n){\mathcal{O}}(1/n) similarly to classic interactive LDP approaches (Smith et al., 2017). Finally, we empirically validate IWP-SGD on binary classification tasks using synthetic and real-world datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method that asymptotically recovers the non-private population risk minimizer in a fully task-agnostic LDP setting using a single privatized release per data point.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We formalize the processing of data released under the Gaussian and Randomized Response mechanisms as transform operators of the intended computations, enabling a unified analysis of their induced bias (Section 3). This view allows us to fully characterize the bias induced by the Gaussian and Randomized Response in standard risk minimization for binary classification (Section 4).

  • •

    We construct an unbiased gradient estimator by inverting the transform associated with gradient computation on LDP records. Using this estimator, we propose Inverse Weierstrass Private SGD (IWP-SGD). We formally analyze IWP-SGD, showing that it recovers, in expectation, the solution to the original problem (Section 5).

  • •

    We empirically evaluate IWP-SGD on synthetic and real-world binary classification tasks, showing that it successfully removes the bias induced by LDP (Section 6).

1.1 Related Work

Interactive LDP Methods.

Interactive methods permit adaptive communication between learners and data owners, with each owner potentially answering multiple sequential queries. A famous example is distributed SGD, where each data owner shares a noisy version of the gradient computed on their local data (Smith et al., 2017; Duchi et al., 2018). It is also the root of private SGD-based algorithms in Wang & Xu (2019) to perform sparse linear regression. As the learner explicitly queries gradient evaluations at successive model updates, these approaches do not permit data reusability and suffer from a large communication cost.

Noninteractive and Task-Specific LDP Methods.

Noninteractive methods, by definition, prohibit adaptive communication: data owners release one or several privatized statistics only once. For example, Wang et al. (2019) and Zheng et al. (2017) tackle the estimation of generalized linear models under LDP using Chebychev and Bernstein polynomial approximations of the loss gradients. These approaches use multiple Gaussian-perturbed versions of each data point to construct a biased gradient estimator for which the bias shrinks with the number of noisy data releases. In Wang et al. (2018), data owners compute noisy loss evaluations over a grid of model values to estimate the population risk, which is optimized later. As a grid-based method, it suffers from an exponential dimension dependency, and loss evaluations are not reusable for other ML problems involving different losses. In contrast, our method only requires one noisy release to construct an unbiased estimator, directly reduces noise variance, while allowing reusing the data for a large class of downstream tasks.

Learning with Noisy Data.

Beyond LDP, several notable works have considered settings where data points are subject to local randomization, although these studies are not directly concerned with privacy. Bishop (1995) approximates the bias induced by Gaussian noise addition in the features as an implicit regularization, while van Rooyen & Williamson (2018) models label corruption identically to the way we model the Randomized Response mechanism in Section 3.2: our bias characterization encompasses both as special cases. Scaman et al. (2024) identifies a learning bias when training and test data distributions differ in a worst-case scenario. Prior works on deconvolution methods (Fan, 1991) aim to recover the density of data from repeated noisy observations. In our work, we do not aim to estimate the noiseless distribution, but directly tackle computations performed on noisy inputs.

Noninteractive and Task-Agnostic LDP.

Several instances of noninteractive and task-agnostic methods exist in the literature. Zheng et al. (2017) study a debiasing method for sparse linear regression, while Wang & Xu (2019) consider the case where only labels are private. Duchi et al. (2018) study the optimal noninteractive and task-agnostic LDP methods for mean and median estimation. Our method proposes a principled solution that generalizes these results to a broader class of learning problems under Gaussian and Randomized Response LDP mechanisms.

2 Privacy Setting and Notations

Notations.

We consider a supervised learning setting with a bounded feature space 𝒳⊂ℝp\mathcal{X}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{p} and a binary label space 𝒴={−1,1}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{-1,1\}. Let 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} be a joint distribution over 𝒳×𝒴{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}, and let (x,y)(x,y) be an example drawn from 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}. We denote by ‖⋅‖\left\|{\cdot}\right\| the euclidean norm and for any subset 𝒵⊂ℝd{\mathcal{Z}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, we write ‖𝒵‖=supz∈𝒵‖z‖\left\|{{\mathcal{Z}}}\right\|=\sup_{z\in{\mathcal{Z}}}\left\|{z}\right\|. The Laplacian of a twice differentiable function ff is Δ⁡[f]=∑i∂xi2[f]\Delta[f]=\sum_{i}\partial^{2}_{x_{i}}[f] and its composition kk times is denoted Δk​[f]=(Δ∘⋯∘Δ)​[f]\Delta^{k}[f]=(\Delta\circ\dots\circ\Delta)[f].

Privacy.

For the remainder of the paper, we consider a privacy setting in which data is released once and for all, without adapting the mechanism to any specific downstream task. We call it the task-agnostic setting. To this end, we leverage Local Differential Privacy, defined as follows.

Definition 2.1 (Local Differential Privacy (LDP) (Kasiviswanathan et al., 2008)).

Let ℳ:E→F{\mathcal{M}}:E\rightarrow F be a randomized algorithm. Let ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0, the mechanism ℳ{\mathcal{M}} satisfies (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP if, for any z,z′∈Ez,z^{\prime}\in E and any subset 𝒞⊆F{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq F,

ℙ⁡(ℳ⁡(z)∈𝒞)≤eϵ​ℙ​(ℳ⁡(z′)∈𝒞)+δ.{\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{M}}(z)\in{\mathcal{C}})\leq e^{\epsilon}{\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{M}}(z^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{C}})+\delta.

If δ=0\delta=0, we say that ℳ{\mathcal{M}} satisfies ϵ\epsilon-LDP.

To enforce LDP, one can use the Gaussian mechanism (Dwork & Roth, 2014) for continuous variables.

Proposition 2.2 (Gaussian Mechanism).

Assume a bounded subset 𝒳⊂ℝp{\mathcal{X}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{p}. By the Gaussian mechanism, the release of

𝒢ϵ,δ​(x)\displaystyle{\mathcal{G}}_{\epsilon,\delta}(x) =x+w,w∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip),\displaystyle=x+w,\quad w\sim{\mathcal{N}}\left(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p}\right),

with σ2=8​log⁡(1.25/δ)​‖𝒳‖2/ϵ2\sigma^{2}=8\log(1.25/\delta)\left\|{{\mathcal{X}}}\right\|^{2}/\epsilon^{2} is (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP.

Similarly, one can use the Randomized Response (Kairouz et al., 2014) to enforce LDP for binary variables.

Proposition 2.3 (Randomized Response (RR)).

Assume 𝒴={−1,1}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{-1,1\}. By the Randomized Response, the release of

ℬϵ​(y)={y​ with probability ​S​(ϵ),−y​ with probability ​ 1−S⁡(ϵ),{\mathcal{B}}_{\epsilon}(y)=\begin{cases}y\;\text{ with probability }\;S(\epsilon)\kern 5.0pt,\\ -y\;\text{ with probability }\;1-S(\epsilon)\kern 5.0pt,\end{cases}

where S⁡(ϵ)=1/(1+e−ϵ)S(\epsilon)=1/(1+e^{-\epsilon}), is ϵ\epsilon-LDP.

Throughout the paper, we consider the following task-agnostic (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP mechanism, which releases continuous features with the Gaussian mechanism, and a binary label with RR. Formally, for an example (x,y)(x,y) drawn from 𝒟{\mathcal{D}},

(x~,y~)\displaystyle(\tilde{x},\;\tilde{y}) =(𝒢ϵx,δ​(x),ℬϵy​(y)).\displaystyle=({\mathcal{G}}_{\epsilon_{x},\delta}(x),\;{\mathcal{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}(y))\kern 5.0pt. (1)

The total privacy guarantee of this mechanism is ϵ=ϵx+ϵy\epsilon=\epsilon_{x}+\epsilon_{y}, combining budgets over features and labels.

3 Privacy as a Transform

When learning from the LDP release defined in Equation (1), any data-dependent quantity, such as a loss or a gradient, can be viewed as a function hh evaluated on a randomized version of the data. Ideally, one would like these quantities to be unbiased, in the sense that their expectation with respect to the privacy noise coincides with the value of hh evaluated on the original data (x,y)(x,y). However, this is generally not the case. Instead, local randomization of data induces a systematic transformation of the function hh. We formalize this with a transform as follows:

𝕋ϵ,δ​[h]:(x,y)↦𝔼(x~,y~)​[h⁡(x~,y~)].{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}[h]:\;(x,\;y)\mapsto{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}[h(\tilde{x},\;\tilde{y})].

This operator maps the original function hh to its average evaluation on noisy releases (x~,y~)(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) of a given data point (x,y)(x,y). This perspective fully captures the effect of local randomization. As a consequence, bias analysis and correction can be carried out by the study of 𝕋ϵ,δ{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta} without any assumptions about the data distribution. In this section, we first study the transforms associated with the Gaussian and Randomized Response mechanisms in isolation. Then, we present how to characterize the joint effect of both mechanisms through the composition of their respective transforms.

3.1 Weierstrass Transform: a Tool for Gaussian Noise

First, we remark that applying a Gaussian noise to the inputs of an arbitrary function and considering the expectation induces a Gaussian smoothing operator known as the Generalized Weierstrass transform (Bilodeau, 1962).

Definition 3.1 (Generalized Weierstrass transform).

Let f:ℝp→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}. The Weierstrass transform is the function 𝕎σ2​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f] defined for any x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p} and σ>0\sigma>0 as

𝕎σ2​[f]​(x)=𝔼w∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip)​[f⁡(x+w)].{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f](x)={\mathbb{E}}_{w\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p})}\left[f(x+w)\right].

The alternative parameterization σ2=2​t\sigma^{2}=2t is commonly used in the literature on the Weierstrass transform. We focus on a class of sufficiently regular functions for which the Weierstrass transform admits a well-defined series representation (Bilodeau, 1962; Eddington, 1913).

Definition 3.2 (Class of Gaussian growing and slowly growing iterated Laplacians function).

For constants M,a>0M,a>0, let ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})} denote the set of infinitely continuously differentiable functions ff from ℝp{\mathbb{R}}^{p} to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} such that for any x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}

|f⁡(x)|\displaystyle|f(x)| ≤M​exp⁡(a​‖x‖2),\displaystyle\leq M\exp(a||x||^{2}), (2)
|Δk​f​(x)|\displaystyle|\Delta^{k}f(x)| ≤Ax⋅(4​a)k​k!,∀k∈ℕ,\displaystyle\leq A_{x}\cdot(4a)^{k}k!,\>\forall k\in{\mathbb{N}}, (3)

for some Ax>0A_{x}>0 that depends only on xx.

Note that (2) requires ff to grow slower than the exponential of a quadratic function, which is a fairly mild condition. The condition (3) is met, for example, for finite linear combinations of exponentials, sines, cosines, polynomials, and band-limited functions. According to a known result in the study of the heat equation (Bilodeau, 1962; Eddington, 1913), the Weierstrass transform of functions in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})} admits the following series expression.

Theorem 3.3 (Series expression of 𝕎σ2{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}).

Let f∈ΦM,a​(ℝp)f\in{\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}. Then, for any σ2<1/2​a\sigma^{2}<1/2a, the generalized Weierstrass transform 𝕎σ2​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f] admits the following expression

𝕎σ2​[f]=∑k=0∞σ2​k2k​k!​Δk​[f].{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}[f]\kern 5.0pt.
Sketch of proof.

The proof is given in Appendix B. First, using the analyticity of the heat equation solution, we remark that 𝕎σ2​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f] is such an analytic solution. With the parameterization σ2=2​t\sigma^{2}=2t, we use the Taylor expression of t↦𝕎2​t​[f]t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f] around a positive t0>0t_{0}>0. We then take the limit as t0t_{0} goes to zero to obtain a formal expression of 𝕎2​t​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f]. Given that ff is in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}, the resulting series converges and we can identify it to 𝕎σ2​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f]. ∎

Remark 3.4.

The condition σ2<1/2​a\sigma^{2}<1/2a is not a strong limitation since, even for fast-increasing functions, aa can be very small. For example, the exponential loss f⁡(x)=exp⁡(−θ⊤​x​y)\smash{f(x)=\exp(-\theta^{\top}xy}) is in ΦMa,a​(ℝp)\smash{\Phi_{M_{a},a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}, with Ma=exp⁡(‖Θ‖2/4​a)\smash{M_{a}=\exp({\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}}/{4a})}, for any (θ,y)∈Θ×𝒴\smash{(\theta,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{Y}}} and any arbitrary small a>0a>0 (see Appendix B.2 for more details).

3.2 Bernoulli Transform: a Tool for Binary Label Noise

We also define the analogous transform associated with the Randomized Response (RR) for an arbitrary real-valued function of binary inputs. The same transform is studied in van Rooyen & Williamson (2018). For clarity, we call it the Bernoulli transform, referencing the random draw of a Bernoulli variable in the RR mechanism.

Definition 3.5 (Bernoulli transform).

Let g:{−1,1}→ℝg:\{-1,1\}\to{\mathbb{R}}, we define for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and any y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\},

𝔹ϵ​[g]​(y)\displaystyle{\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon}[g](y) =𝔼ℬϵ​[g⁡(ℬϵ​(y))]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{\epsilon}}\left[g({\mathcal{B}}_{\epsilon}(y))\right]
=S⁡(ϵ)​g​(y)+(1−S⁡(ϵ))​g​(−y).\displaystyle=S(\epsilon)g(y)+(1-S(\epsilon))g(-y).

The Bernoulli transform is the expected value of a function of a binary data point yy under the Randomized Response mechanism with a given privacy budget ϵ\epsilon.

3.3 Combining Weierstrass and Bernoulli Transforms

When computing a function h:𝒳×𝒴→ℝh:{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}\to{\mathbb{R}} of continuous and binary variables, we can compose the transforms defined for both the Gaussian and RR mechanisms as follows:

𝕋ϵ,δ​[h]​(x,y)\displaystyle{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}[h](x,y) =𝔼(x~,y~)​[h​(x~,y~)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[h\left(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}\right)\right] (4)
=𝔹ϵy[z↦𝕎σ2[h(⋅,z)](x)](y).\displaystyle={\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}\left[z\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[h(\cdot,z)](x)\right](y).

This transform accounts for the simultaneous effect of Gaussian noise on continuous variables and sign flipping on labels. It will allow to analyze the combined effects of Gaussian and Randomized Response mechanisms on the population risk in binary classification.

4 Bias in Risk Minimization

We now turn to the learning problem and study how task-agnostic LDP affects the outcome of risk minimization. In particular, we focus on the bias incurred by LDP when the goal is to learn the minimizer of the true population risk directly. This is essential as such bias is intrinsic to the problem at hand, and cannot be compensated for by increasing the number of records used for training. Depending on the settings, LDP noise may or may not change the population risk minimizer. When it does not, the original population risk minimizer can be recovered, provided that enough samples are available. In some other problems, however, the injected noise modifies the expected loss, resulting in a biased minimizer that might be far from the original model. When this occurs, increasing the sample size is not sufficient to eliminate the discrepancy between the learned solution and the true population risk minimizer.

In this section, we study the population risk obtained when losses are evaluated on task-agnostic LDP releases generated by the Gaussian and RR mechanisms. By expressing the expected noisy loss as the composition of the Weierstrass and Bernoulli transforms, we explicitly characterize when and how these mechanisms shift the population risk.

Risk Minimization.

Let Θ⊂ℝk\Theta\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{k} be a bounded convex set of model parameters. Let ℓ:Θ×ℝp×𝒴→ℝ\ell:\Theta\times{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\times{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} be a real-valued function defined for any tuple (θ,x,y)∈Θ×𝒳×𝒴(\theta,x,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}} as the loss incurred when predicting an example with features xx using a model θ\theta, given that the true label is yy. We can then evaluate the quality of any model θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta with the population risk ℛ{\mathcal{R}}, defined as follows:

ℛ⁡(θ)=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​[ℓ⁡(θ,x,y)].{\mathcal{R}}(\theta)={\mathbb{E}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}}[\ell(\theta,x,y)].

For the remainder of the paper, we consider loss functions satisfying the following regularity assumption.

Assumption 4.1 (Loss regularity).

The functions x↦ℓ⁡(θ,x,y)x\mapsto\ell(\theta,x,y) and x↦∂θjℓ⁡(θ,x,y)x\mapsto\partial_{\theta_{j}}\ell(\theta,x,y) for j∈{1,…,k}j\in\{1,\dots,k\} are in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})} (see Definition 3.2) for any (θ,y)∈Θ×𝒴(\theta,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{Y}}.

Bias in Noisy Risk Minimization.

Let ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0, for any model θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, we define the expected population risk when the loss is evaluated on the (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP release of (x,y)(x,y) defined in Equation (1) as follows:

ℛ~​(θ)\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{R}}(\theta) =𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​𝔼(x~,y~)​[ℓ⁡(θ,x~,y~)].\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[\ell(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\right].

We first analyze the pointwise loss 𝔼(x~,y~)​[ℓ⁡(θ,x~,y~)]{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[\ell(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\right] for a given pair (x,y)(x,y) and model θ\theta. Recalling Equation (4) with h⁡(⋅,⋅)=ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)h(\cdot,\cdot)=\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot), we have

𝔼(x~,y~)​[ℓ⁡(θ,x~,y~)]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[\ell\left(\theta,\;\tilde{x},\;\tilde{y}\right)\right] =𝕋ϵ,δ​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(x,y).\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](x,y). (5)

Developing the expression of the composed transform 𝕋ϵ,δ{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta} and averaging over (x,y)∼𝒟(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}} yields a relation between the noisy population risk ℛ~\tilde{\mathcal{R}} and the original population risk ℛ{\mathcal{R}} in the following theorem (proven in Appendix C).

Theorem 4.2 (Bias induced by the Gaussian and Randomized Response mechanisms in binary classification).

Let Δx\Delta_{x} denote the Laplacian with respect to the variable xx and assume that ℓ\ell satisfies Assumption 4.1 with a<1/2​σ2a<1/2\sigma^{2}. Recall S⁡(ϵy)=1/(1+e−ϵy)S(\epsilon_{y})=1/(1+e^{-\epsilon_{y}}). For any θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta,

ℛ~​(θ)−\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{R}}(\theta)- ℛ⁡(θ)=(1−S⁡(ϵy))​(𝔼x,y​[ℓ⁡(θ,x,−y)]−ℛ⁡(θ))⏟label noise contribution\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}(\theta)=\underbrace{\left(1-S(\epsilon_{y})\right)\left({\mathbb{E}}_{x,y}\left[\ell(\theta,x,-y)\right]-{\mathcal{R}}(\theta)\right)}_{\text{label noise contribution}}
+S⁡(ϵy)​∑k=1∞σ2​k2k​k!​𝔼x,y​[Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,y)]⏟feature noise contribution\displaystyle+S(\epsilon_{y})\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}{\mathbb{E}}_{x,y}\left[\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y)\right]}_{\text{feature noise contribution}}
+(1−S⁡(ϵy))​∑k=1∞σ2​k2k​k!​𝔼x,y​[Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,−y)]⏟interactions of feature and label noise.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\left(1-S(\epsilon_{y})\right)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}{\mathbb{E}}_{x,y}\left[\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,-y)\right]}_{\text{interactions of feature and label noise}}.

Theorem 4.2 shows that Randomized Response on labels induces a mixture between the risks associated with true and corrupted labels, while Gaussian feature noise induces a systematic smoothing of the loss through iterated Laplacians. For non-private labels (ϵy→∞)(\epsilon_{y}\to\infty), our result admits the work of Bishop (1995), proposed in the more restrictive low noise regime, as a particular case. Indeed, the loss functions they consider admit a second-order Taylor approximation with respect to the features and they derive an approximate expression of the expected risk on noisy data that matches exactly ours truncated at k=1k=1. For non-private features (ϵx→∞)(\epsilon_{x}\to\infty), we recover the corruption of labels in van Rooyen & Williamson (2018).

For some specific loss functions, the bias term in Theorem 4.2 has a closed-form expression. For instance, if the derivatives of ℓ\ell with respect to the features vanish after a certain order, then ℛ~\tilde{\mathcal{R}} reduces to a finite sum. Even for infinitely differentiable loss functions ℓ\ell with non-zero derivatives, we can sometimes derive a closed-form expression of the bias. This is, for example, the case for the exponential loss.

Example 1 (Exponential loss).

Consider ℓ⁡(θ,x,y)=exp⁡(−θ⊤​x​y)\ell(\theta,x,y)=\exp(-\theta^{\top}xy), we have for any θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta,

ℛ~​(θ)=eσ2​‖θ‖2/2​(S⁡(ϵy)​ℛ​(θ)+(1−S⁡(ϵy))​ℛ​(−θ)).\tilde{\mathcal{R}}(\theta)=e^{\sigma^{2}\|\theta\|^{2}/2}\left(S(\epsilon_{y}){\mathcal{R}}(\theta)+(1-S(\epsilon_{y})){\mathcal{R}}(-\theta)\right).

Define θ~∗∈arg⁡minθ​ℛ~​(θ)\tilde{\theta}^{*}\in\arg\min_{\theta}\tilde{\mathcal{R}}(\theta) and θ∗∈arg⁡minθ⁡ℛ⁡(θ)\theta^{*}\in\arg\min_{\theta}{\mathcal{R}}(\theta), applying the logarithm preserves the minimum so θ~∗\tilde{\theta}^{*} also minimizes

log⁡(S⁡(ϵy)​ℛ​(θ)+(1−S⁡(ϵy))​ℛ​(−θ))+σ22​‖θ‖2.\displaystyle\log\left(S(\epsilon_{y}){\mathcal{R}}\left(\theta\right)+(1-S(\epsilon_{y})){\mathcal{R}}\left(-\theta\right)\right)+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}.

The term in ‖θ‖2\|\theta\|^{2} can be seen as further regularization induced by the feature noise, while the term ℛ⁡(−θ){\mathcal{R}}(-\theta) promotes predicting the wrong label in some cases due to label contamination. Both of these effects steer the optimal solution away from θ∗\theta^{*}, creating a gap between θ∗\theta^{*} and θ~∗\tilde{\theta}^{*}. We exhibit this gap empirically in Figure 1 and 2 in Section 6.

Note that, considering 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} as an empirical distribution over a dataset of nn examples leads to the same bias characterization in empirical risk minimization. Having characterized the population risk bias induced when learning from (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP published examples from Gaussian and RR mechanisms under the lens of the Weierstrass and Bernoulli transforms, we now turn to the natural next step of correcting it.

5 Bias Correction

In this section, we leverage the framework of privacy seen as a transform introduced in Section 3 to design a practical method that corrects the bias we identified in the previous section. To this end, we start by defining the inverse of the aforementioned transforms.

Theorem 5.1 (Inverse of 𝔹ϵ{\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon} and 𝕎σ2{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}).

Define S~​(ϵ)=1/(1−e−ϵ)\tilde{S}(\epsilon)=1/(1-e^{-\epsilon}). Let g:𝒴→ℝg:{\mathcal{Y}}\to{\mathbb{R}} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, for any y~∈𝒴\tilde{y}\in{\mathcal{Y}},

  1. (i)

    𝔹ϵ−1​[g]​(y~)=S~​(ϵ)​g​(y~)+(1−S~​(ϵ))​g​(−y~){\mathbb{B}}^{-1}_{\epsilon}[g](\tilde{y})=\tilde{S}(\epsilon)g(\tilde{y})+\big(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon)\big)g(-\tilde{y}).

Let f∈ΦM,a​(ℝp)f\in{\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}, for any σ2<1/4​a\sigma^{2}<1/4a and x~∈ℝp\tilde{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}

  1. (ii)

    𝕎σ2−1​[f]​(x~)=∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​Δk​[f]​(x~).{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}_{\sigma^{2}}[f](\tilde{x})=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}[f](\tilde{x}).

Proofs of the two inverse transforms can be found in Appendix D.1. Remark that σ2\sigma^{2} is lower than 1/4​a1/4a instead of 1/2​a1/2a. That is because to prove that 𝕎σ2−1{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1} is the inverse of 𝕎σ2{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}, we apply a composition of their two series expression, resulting in a stronger constraint on σ2\sigma^{2}. Computing 𝔹−1​[g]{\mathbb{B}}^{-1}[g] requires two evaluations of gg and matches the noisy label correction in van Rooyen & Williamson (2018, Theorem 5). 𝕎−1​[f]{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}[f] can be computed by deriving a closed-form expression (see Section 5.2) or approximated by truncating the sum (see Appendix D.7).

The invertibility of these transforms plays a fundamental role in our study: when computing the inverse transform on noisy data, we obtain an unbiased estimate of the original function. Indeed, taking the expectation of 𝕎σ2−1​[f]​(x~){\mathbb{W}}^{-1}_{\sigma^{2}}[f](\tilde{x}) (resp. 𝔹ϵ−1​[g]​(y~){\mathbb{B}}^{-1}_{\epsilon}[g](\tilde{y})) amounts to computing the Weierstrass (resp. Bernoulli) transform, which recovers the function on the original data record xx (resp. yy). Next, we will show that these two transforms can be applied and inverted sequentially, which will allow us to build novel, unbiased estimators of gradients of binary classification losses.

Composition of 𝔹−1{\mathbb{B}}^{-1} and 𝕎−1{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}.

For any function h:ℝp×𝒴→ℝh:{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\times{\mathcal{Y}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, the inverse of 𝕋ϵ,δ{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta} is

𝕋ϵ,δ−1[h](x~,y~)=𝔹ϵy−1[z↦𝕎σ2−1[h(⋅,z)](x~)](y~).\displaystyle{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1}[h](\tilde{x},\tilde{y})={\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}^{-1}\left[z\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1}[h(\cdot,z)](\tilde{x})\right](\tilde{y}).

It provides a basis for the definition of the following unbiased loss estimator from (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP releases via Gaussian and Randomized Response mechanisms, we call the Inverse Weierstrass Private (IWP) loss estimator:

ℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)=𝕋ϵ,δ−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(x~,y~).\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})={\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](\tilde{x},\tilde{y}). (6)

We differentiate it to obtain the IWP gradient estimator

∇θℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)=𝕋ϵ,δ−1​[∇θℓ​(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(x~,y~),\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})={\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1}[\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](\tilde{x},\tilde{y}), (7)

with the convention that 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} and 𝕋−1{\mathbb{T}}^{-1} act component-wise on vector-valued functions such as the gradient. We show in Appendix D.2 that the IWP gradient estimator is indeed the gradient of the IWP loss estimator.

The following theorem, proven in Appendix D.3, states the unbiasedness guarantees of both ℓ~ϵ,δ\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta} and ∇θℓ~ϵ,δ\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}.

Theorem 5.2 (Unbiasedness of IWP loss and gradient estimators).

Assume ℓ\ell satisfies Assumption 4.1 with a<1/4​σ2a<1/4\sigma^{2}. Let ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0, for any pair (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}} and θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, define (x~,y~)(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) as a (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP release defined in Equation (1), the IWP loss estimator defined in Equation (6) satisfies:

  • (i)

    𝔼(x~,y~)​[ℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)]=ℓ⁡(θ,x,y){\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\right]=\ell(\theta,x,y),

  • (ii)

    𝔼(x~,y~)​[∇θℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)]=∇θℓ​(θ,x,y){\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\right]=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,x,y).

Using the IWP gradient estimator, we introduce IWP-SGD in Algorithm 1. It is a single-pass projected SGD over a dataset D~n={(x~i,y~i)}i=1n\tilde{D}_{n}=\{(\tilde{x}_{i},\tilde{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} consisting of (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta) releases of samples (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) drawn i.i.d. from 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}. It relies on the update θt=ΠΘ​(θt−1+γ​∇θℓ~ϵ,δ​(θt,x~t,y~t))\theta_{t}=\Pi_{\Theta}\left(\theta_{t-1}+\gamma\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta_{t},\tilde{x}_{t},\tilde{y}_{t})\right) for each tt in {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\}, with γ>0\gamma>0, θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta and ΠΘ\Pi_{\Theta} the projection on Θ\Theta.

Following standard convergence analyses of SGD with unbiased stochastic gradient, we bound the variance of the IWP gradient estimator in the following theorem.

Theorem 5.3 (Variance of the IWP gradient estimator).

Let ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0, an original feature-label pair x,y∈𝒳×𝒴x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}} and its corresponding (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP release (x~,y~)(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) defined in Equation (1). Let ℓ\ell satisfy Assumption 4.1 with a<1/4​σ2a<1/4\sigma^{2}. Given that 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} and Θ\Theta are bounded sets, denoting

C\displaystyle C =sup(θ,x,y)∈Θ×𝒳×𝒴,s<σ2max{‖∇θℓ(θ,x,y)‖,\displaystyle=\sup_{(\theta,x,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}},s<\sigma^{2}}\max\Big\{\left\|{\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,x,y)}\right\|, (8)
‖𝕎s−1[∇θ∇xℓ(θ,⋅,y)](x)‖},\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\left\|{{\mathbb{W}}_{s}^{-1}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\nabla_{x}\ell(\theta,\cdot,y)\right](x)}\right\|\Big\},

the variance of the IWP gradient estimator admits the following upper bound

𝔼​‖∇θℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)−∇θℓ​(θ,x,y)‖2\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left\|{\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})-\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,x,y)}\right\|^{2}
≤C2​(σ2+4​S~​(ϵy)​(S~​(ϵy)−1)​(1+σ2)).\displaystyle\quad\leq C^{2}\left(\sigma^{2}+4\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\left(\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})-1\right)(1+\sigma^{2})\right)\kern 5.0pt. (9)
Sketch of proof.

The proof is given in Appendix D.4. We prove the result using a combination of the marginal variances from both x~\tilde{x} and y~\tilde{y} together with total variance law. It yields an exact variance expression that we can bound using Equation (8), relying on the increasing property of 𝕎σ2{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}} proven in Appendix B.2. ∎

The resulting variance bound in Theorem 5.3 distinguishes the three contributions of 𝕎−1{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}, 𝔹−1{\mathbb{B}}^{-1}, and the compound contribution of both in the resulting variance. It shows dependency in the feature noise variance and labels privacy budget ϵy\epsilon_{y}. A dependency on the loss can be further quantified via the constant CC. Indeed, the growth rate of CC with ‖𝒳‖\left\|{{\mathcal{X}}}\right\| and ‖Θ‖\left\|{\Theta}\right\| is affected by the regularity of the loss. For example, for the quadratic loss with linear models, CC is of order 𝒪⁡(p​‖𝒳‖​‖Θ‖){\mathcal{O}}(p\left\|{{\mathcal{X}}}\right\|\left\|{\Theta}\right\|). Similarly, for the exponential loss with linear models, CC is of order 𝒪⁡(exp⁡(ϵx2)​(p+‖𝒳‖​‖Θ‖+σ2​‖Θ‖2)){\mathcal{O}}\big(\exp\big(\epsilon_{x}^{2}\big)\big(p+\left\|{{\mathcal{X}}}\right\|\left\|{\Theta}\right\|+\sigma^{2}\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}\big)\big) (see proofs in Appendix D.6). Now that we have bounded the variance of the IWP gradient estimator, we can analyze the IWP-SGD convergence guarantees using known results on SGD with unbiased stochastic gradients.

5.1 Convergence guarantees of IWP-SGD

We give convergence guarantees of IWP-SGD under the strong convexity and smoothness assumptions (see Appendix A for proper definitions).

Assumption 5.4 (Strong convexity and smoothness).

ℛ{\mathcal{R}} is μ\mu-strongly convex and 𝒦{\mathcal{K}}-smooth, with 𝒦>0{\mathcal{K}}>0 and μ>0\mu>0.

These assumptions are common in the analysis of SGD’s convergence (Moulines & Bach, 2011; Stich, 2019) and are used solely for this purpose in this paper.

Theorem 5.5 (Convergence guarantees of IWP-SGD).

Let ℓ\ell satisfy Assumption 4.1 and be such that ℛ{\mathcal{R}} satisfies Assumption 5.4. Let the privacy budget be ϵ=ϵx+ϵy,δ>0\epsilon=\epsilon_{x}+\epsilon_{y},\;\delta>0 such that σ2<1/4​a\sigma^{2}<1/4a. Denote θ∗=arg⁡minθ⁡ℛ⁡(θ)\theta^{*}=\arg\min_{\theta}{\mathcal{R}}(\theta). Assume 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} and Θ\Theta are bounded convex sets and let CC be as defined in Equation (8). For any n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} the number of training samples, initial model θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta and step-size γ≤12​𝒦\gamma\leq\frac{1}{2{\mathcal{K}}}, Algorithm 1 is (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP and its output θn\theta_{n} satisfies

𝔼|θn−\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\|\theta_{n}- θ∗∥2≤(1−γμ)n∥θ0−θ∗∥2\displaystyle\theta^{*}\|^{2}\leq(1-\gamma\mu)^{n}\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{*}\|^{2}
+𝒪⁡(γ​C2μ​S~​(ϵy)​(S~​(ϵy)−1)​log⁡(1.25/δ)ϵx2).\displaystyle+{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\gamma C^{2}}{\mu}\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\left(\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})-1\right)\frac{\log(1.25/\delta)}{\epsilon_{x}^{2}}\right).

In addition, for an appropriate step size γ=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n)/n)\gamma={\mathcal{O}}(\log(n)/n),

𝔼|θn−\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\|\theta_{n}- θ∗∥2≤𝒪~(∥θ0−θ∗∥2exp(−μ​n2​𝒦))\displaystyle\theta^{*}\|^{2}\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{*}\|^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu n}{2{\mathcal{K}}}\right)\right)
+𝒪~​(C2μ2​n​S~​(ϵy)​(S~​(ϵy)−1)​log⁡(1.25/δ)ϵx2),\displaystyle+\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{C^{2}}{\mu^{2}n}\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\left(\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})-1\right)\frac{\log(1.25/\delta)}{\epsilon_{x}^{2}}\right),

where 𝒪~\tilde{\mathcal{O}} hides logarithmic terms in nn.

Sketch of proof.

The proof, given in Appendix D.8, is a direct application of Stich (2019) with our unbiased noisy gradient estimator and its variance bound given in Theorem 5.3. We also use their derivation for the appropriate step-size γ=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n)/n)\gamma={\mathcal{O}}(\log(n)/n). ∎

Theorem 5.5 shows that the last iterate of IWP-SGD is converging to the population risk minimizer when the number of examples grows to infinity. The convergence rate of IWP-SGD matches the dependency on nn of locally private SGD in Smith et al. (2017, Theorem 20, item 4). However, depending on the choice of loss, we may, through CC, suffer from a higher dependency on the dimensions of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} and Θ\Theta than Smith et al. (2017), which, for 1-Lipschitz, smooth and strongly-convex losses, show a linear dependency on the dimension of the model space Θ\Theta. In practice, one can obtain estimators with lower variance by considering batches of examples at each iteration. However, it does not change the fact that each example can only be used once in the optimization process, and, thus, has limited impact on the total number of records required to approximate the solution.

The general framework of IWP-SGD can be instantiated in various settings. In particular, when applied to generalized linear models, the method admits a more tractable form, which we develop in the following subsection.

5.2 Application to Generalized Linear Models

Let ℓ⁡(θ,x,y)=f⁡(θ⊤​x​y)\ell(\theta,x,y)=f\left(\theta^{\top}xy\right) be a loss that satisfies the generalized linear loss assumption. In this case, by Equation (6), the IWP loss estimators becomes

ℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)\displaystyle\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\;\tilde{x},\;\tilde{y}) =S~​(ϵy)​𝕎σ2​‖θ‖2−1​[f]​(θ⊤​x~​y~)\displaystyle=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y}){\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}}^{-1}[f]\left(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\right)

and the IWP gradient estimator can be expressed as

∇θℓ~ϵ,δ​(θCLOSE,\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta, OPENx~,y~)=S~​(ϵy)​∇θ𝕎σ2​‖θ‖2−1​[f]​(θ⊤​x~​y~)\displaystyle\tilde{x},\tilde{y})=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}}^{-1}[f]\left(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\right)

This form involves the Weierstrass transform of the scalar valued function ff instead of ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,y)\ell(\theta,\cdot,y), which simplifies the IWP gradient estimator expression. It further yields a closed-form expression for some losses ff such as the quadratic or exponential losses.

6 Experiments

This section empirically validates the claimed guarantees of convergence and absence of bias of Section 5. We compare three different SGD approaches: (i) SGD - real data: on the original dataset without noise, (ii) SGD - noisy data: on the (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP released dataset via the mechanism of Equation (1) and (iii) IWP-SGD: Algorithm 1 on the same (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP released dataset. All the experiments are binary classification problems with linear models minimizing the exponential loss with ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization. It is thus a strongly convex problem having a unique minimizer. We average 100 random draws of data and noise of the LDP mechanism for the synthetic data, and noise only for the real data. Across all three methods, we report the empirical risk on a test dataset defined as ℒ⁡(θ)=1n​∑iℓ⁡(θ,xi,yi){\mathcal{L}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\ell(\theta,x_{i},y_{i}). Additional details on the experimental setup are provided in Appendix E.

Synthetic Data.

We study two synthetic binary classification problems in dimension p=2p=2 and p=10p=10 generated with the make_classification routine of scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) having features within [−1,1]p[-1,1]^{p}. We conduct the experiments on n=106n=10^{6} samples for two privacy guarantees : (2,10−5)(2,10^{-5})-LDP for p=2p=2 and (5,10−5)(5,10^{-5})-LDP for p=10p=10.

The constant loss over the batches in Figure 1 shows models fitted via SGD on noisy data converge to a different model than models fitted via SGD on the real data. Whereas the loss of models fitted via IWP-SGD follow the one of the models fitted on the real data. It illustrates the absence of bias for IWP-SGD and its presence for SGD on noisy data.

Real Data.

We study the ACSIncome and ACSPublicCoverage problems of the Folktables dataset (Ding et al., 2021). ACSIncome consists of predicting whether an individual’s income is above $50 000 and ACSPublicCoverage consists of predicting individual coverage from health insurance. For both problems, we select the three variables AGEP (age in years), SEX and SCHL (educational attainment). For ACSIncome we add WKHP (usual hours worked per week over the past year) and for ACSPublicCoverage we add PINCP (total annual income). We employ the Gaussian mechanism, which is suitable for continuous and ordinal variables. Although suboptimal for binary variables, we also apply it to the SEX attribute for consistency and practicality. We merge the data of the five largest states yielding datasets of respectively 668 859 rows and 883 984 rows for ACSIncome and ACSPublicCoverage. The data is then randomly split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets.

Figure 2 shows the average loss over fitted models (θn)\left(\theta_{n}\right) and also the loss of the averaged model (𝔼​θn)\left({\mathbb{E}}\theta_{n}\right) over the random draws. It allows us to distinguish the remaining excess risk resulting from bias or variance of the IWP-SGD outputs. As with synthetic data, we remark that the constant loss of models fitted via SGD on noisy data with the number of batches illustrates the presence of bias in this setting. Whereas the IWP-SGD outputs are showing a decrease to a remaining low loss close to the one on real data. We can interpret this remaining gap as a consequence of the variance of IWP-SGD. Indeed, on the second plot, the averaged output model (𝔼​θn)\left({\mathbb{E}}\theta_{n}\right) for IWP-SGD is showing a null difference with the loss of the optimal model obtained through SGD.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we characterized the bias that occurs when learning from an LDP-released dataset using Gaussian and Randomized Response mechanisms. Linking these mechanisms with transform operators, we derived an expression of the bias on the population risk under these LDP mechanisms. This view of privacy as a transform yielded the construction of a theoretically-grounded debiasing technique, which takes the form of a variant of SGD called IWP-SGD.

Our results show, theoretically and empirically, that the bias induced by the use of private noisy examples for SGD can be avoided at the cost of a higher variance of the noisy gradient estimator, illustrating a bias-variance tradeoff. This opens a pathway to study LDP through the lens of transform operators. Extending the framework of this paper to other locally private mechanisms presents promising avenues for future exploration.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work that can help in the design of Machine Learning projects using locally private examples. It can help argue against the idea that directly learning from noisy examples in Differential Privacy is a problem that is too hard to be solved using practical algorithms. Future societal consequences might be the publication of locally private data for later use in fields where no public dataset exist.

Appendix A Definitions and Theorems

Notations.

We recall the main notations of the paper:

  • •

    Data lies in 𝒳⊂ℝp\mathcal{X}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, 𝒴={−1,1}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{-1,1\}, parameters in Θ⊂ℝk\Theta\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{k}, and 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} is a joint distribution over 𝒳×𝒴{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}.

    The loss function is ℓ:Θ×ℝp×𝒴→ℝ\ell:\Theta\times{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\times{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} and the associated risk ℛ⁡(θ)=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​[ℓ⁡(θ,x,y)]{\mathcal{R}}(\theta)={\mathbb{E}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}}[\ell(\theta,x,y)].

    We denote ‖⋅‖\left\|{\cdot}\right\| the euclidean norm, and for any subset 𝒵⊂ℝd{\mathcal{Z}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, we write ‖𝒵‖=supz∈𝒵‖z‖\left\|{{\mathcal{Z}}}\right\|=\sup_{z\in{\mathcal{Z}}}\left\|{z}\right\|.

  • •

    For a,b:ℕ→ℝ+a,b:{\mathbb{N}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+}, we write a=𝒪⁡(b)a={\mathcal{O}}(b) if there exists C>0C>0 such that for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, a⁡(n)≤C​b​(n)a(n)\leq Cb(n).

  • •

    For a complex number z=α+i​βz=\alpha+i\beta with (α,β)∈ℝ2(\alpha,\beta)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} and i2=−1i^{2}=-1, we denote ℜ⁡(z)=α\Re(z)=\alpha its real part, ℑ⁡(z)=β\Im(z)=\beta its imaginary part, and |z|=α2+β2|z|=\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}} its modulus.

Subsets of ℝ𝒅\boldsymbol{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}.

We also recall some definitions on subsets of ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} for completeness.

Definition A.1 (Convex subset of ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}).

A subset 𝒵⊂ℝd{\mathcal{Z}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is convex if for any z,z′∈𝒵z,z^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Z}} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], t​z+(1−t)​z′∈𝒵tz+(1-t)z^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Z}}.

Definition A.2 (Open and closed subsets of ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}).

A subset 𝒵⊂ℝd{\mathcal{Z}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is open if for any z∈𝒵z\in{\mathcal{Z}}, there exist δ>0\delta>0 such that for any z~∈ℝd\tilde{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} such that ‖z−z~‖<δ\left\|{z-\tilde{z}}\right\|<\delta, z~∈𝒵\tilde{z}\in{\mathcal{Z}}. The set 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}} is said to be closed if {z∈ℝd|z∉𝒵}\{z\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\>|\>z\notin{\mathcal{Z}}\} is open.

Definition A.3 (Compact subset of ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}).

A subset 𝒵⊂ℝd{\mathcal{Z}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is said to be compact if it is closed and bounded (‖𝒵‖<∞\left\|{{\mathcal{Z}}}\right\|<\infty).

Regularity of functions.

We now define classical regularity definitions for real-valued functions.

Definition A.4 (Convexity and strong convexity).

A differentiable function f:ℝp→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\to{\mathbb{R}} is μ\mu-strongly convex (where μ>0\mu>0) if ∀x,y∈ℝp\forall x,y\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, we have f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)≥⟨∇f​(y),x−y⟩+μ2​‖x−y‖2f(x)-f(y)\geq\langle\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-y\|^{2}, and convex if this holds for μ=0\mu=0.

Definition A.5 (Smoothness).

A differentiable function f:ℝp→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\to{\mathbb{R}} is 𝒦{\mathcal{K}}-smooth if ∀x,x′∈ℝp\forall x,x^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, we have ‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(x′)‖≤𝒦​‖x−x′‖\left\|{\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(x^{\prime})}\right\|\leq{\mathcal{K}}\|x-x^{\prime}\|.

Definition A.6 (Laplacian).

The Laplacian of a twice differentiable function ff is Δ⁡[f]=∑i∂xi2[f]\Delta[f]=\sum_{i}\partial^{2}_{x_{i}}[f] and its composition kk times is denoted Δk​[f]=(Δ∘⋯∘Δ)​[f]\Delta^{k}[f]=(\Delta\circ\dots\circ\Delta)[f].

Analytic functions.

We define real and complex analytic functions as follows.

Definition A.7 (Real analytic functions (Komatsu, 1960)).

A function f:ℝ→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is real analytic on a subset Ω⊂ℝ\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}} if it is infinitely continuously differentiable on Ω\Omega and for any compact K⊂ΩK\subset\Omega, there exist A>0A>0 such that for any k∈ℕ∗k\in{\mathbb{N}}^{*},

supx∈K|dk​fd​xk​(x)|≤Ak+1​k!.\sup_{x\in K}\left|\frac{d^{k}f}{dx^{k}}(x)\right|\leq A^{k+1}k!\kern 5.0pt.
Definition A.8 (Complex analytic function (Ahlfors, 1979)).

A function f:ℂ→ℂf:{\mathbb{C}}\to{\mathbb{C}} is complex analytic on a subset K⊂ℂK\subset{\mathbb{C}} if for any x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega, it admits a convergent power series in a neighborhood of x0x_{0}.

Two key results from complex analysis are Morera’s theorem (Ahlfors, 1979, Page 122) and Cauchy’s integral theorem (Ahlfors, 1979, Theorem 2, Page 109). These will allow us to give explicit expressions of the Weierstrass transform.

Theorem A.9 (Morera’s theorem).

Let f:ℂ→ℂf:{\mathbb{C}}\to{\mathbb{C}} be a complex-valued function that is continuous on K⊂ℂK\subset{\mathbb{C}} an open set in the complex plane. If

∮Γf⁡(x)​𝑑x=0\oint_{\Gamma}f(x)dx=0

for every closed piecewise smooth contour Γ\Gamma in KK, then ff is complex analytic.

Theorem A.10 (Cauchy’s integral theorem).

Let f:ℂ→ℂf:{\mathbb{C}}\to{\mathbb{C}} be a complex analytic function on K⊂ℂK\subset{\mathbb{C}} an open set in the complex plane. Then for any closed piecewise smooth contour Γ\Gamma in KK

∮Γf⁡(x)​𝑑x=0.\oint_{\Gamma}f(x)dx=0.

In particular, a corollary of these two theorems is that for a continuous complex function f:ℂ→ℂf:{\mathbb{C}}\to{\mathbb{C}}, it holds that

f​ is analytic on K⊂ℂ if and only if ​∮Γf⁡(x)​𝑑x=0, for any closed piecewise smooth contour ​Γ⊂K.f\text{ is analytic on $K\subset{\mathbb{C}}$}\textit{ if and only if }\oint_{\Gamma}f(x)dx=0,\text{ for any closed piecewise smooth contour }\Gamma\subset K\kern 5.0pt.

B.1 Expression of the Weierstrass Transform – Proof of Theorem 3.3

We provide a proof of the following theorem, which gives an expression of the Weierstrass transform. See 3.3

To prove this theorem, we use the following lemma from Fritz (1991, Chapter 7, Problem 3). No proof is given for this problem in the initial textbook, we thus provide one in the following.

Lemma B.1 (t↦𝕎2​tt\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t} is analytic for continuous Gaussian growing functions).

Let f:ℝp→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\to{\mathbb{R}} a continuous function satisfying Equation (2) we refer to as Gaussian growth and recall: |f⁡(x)|≤M​exp⁡(a​‖x‖2)|f(x)|\leq M\exp(a\left\|{x}\right\|^{2}), for any x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}. The overall goal is to show the analyticity of t↦𝕎2​t​[f]​(x)t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f](x) on the larger complex domain Ω={t∈ℂs.t.ℜ(1/4t)>a}\Omega=\{t\in\mathbb{C}\;s.t.\;\Re(1/4t)>a\} which contains the real interval ]0,1/4​a[]0,1/4a[. The analyticity of t↦𝕎2​t​[f]​(x)t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f](x) on Ω\Omega is shown by verifying it is analytic on any compact subset K⊂ΩK\subset\Omega. This latter objective is done using Morera’s theorem (see Theorem A.9). We must then verify two properties:

  • (i)

    t↦𝕎2​t​[f]​(x)t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f](x) is continuous on KK,

By Morera’s theorem, if these conditions are met, the function t↦𝕎2​t​[f]​(x)t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f](x) is analytic on KK.

↓Denoting DK,x,a=M​CK​exp⁡((a+δ)​‖x‖2​2​a+δδ)\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small Denoting $D_{K,x,a}=MC_{K}\exp\left((a+\delta)\left\|{x}\right\|^{2}\frac{2a+\delta}{\delta}\right)$}}}
≤DK,x,a​exp⁡(−(δ/2)​‖w‖2),\displaystyle\leq D_{K,x,a}\exp(-(\delta/2)\left\|{w}\right\|^{2})\kern 5.0pt,

which is a scaled Gaussian function, and is thus integrable. Then, for the given x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, w↦F⁡(t,x,w)w\mapsto F(t,x,w) is uniformly dominated by an integrable function for any t∈Kt\in K. So t↦𝕎2​t​[f]t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f] is continuous on KK.

(ii) Morera’s criterion. Let Γ\Gamma be a closed piecewise smooth contour in KK. Then, by Morera’s theorem 𝕎2​t​[f]​(x){\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f](x) is analytic on any arbitrary K⊂ΩK\subset\Omega. Finally, t↦𝕎2​t​[f]​(x)t\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}[f](x) is analytic on Ω\Omega (and in particular on the real interval ]0,1/4​a[]0,1/4a[). ∎

Using this lemma, we now prove Theorem 3.3.

B.2 Weierstrass Transform Properties

We now give two useful properties of the Weierstrass transform.

Proposition B.2 (Linearity of 𝕎σ2{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}).

Let σ>0\sigma>0, the Weierstrass transform is linear with respect to the function it applies to. Let ff and gg be two functions from ℝp{\mathbb{R}}^{p} to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and let α∈ℝ\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}},

𝕎σ2​[α​f+g]=α​𝕎σ2​[f]+𝕎σ2​[g].{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[\alpha f+g]=\alpha{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f]+{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[g].
Proof.

By linearity of the expectation, for a given x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p},

𝕎σ2​[α​f+g]​(x)\displaystyle{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[\alpha f+g](x) =𝔼w∈𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip)​[α​f​(x+w)+g⁡(x+w)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{w\in{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p})}\left[\alpha f(x+w)+g(x+w)\right]
=α​𝔼w∈𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip)​[f⁡(x+w)]+𝔼w∈𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip)​[g⁡(x+w)]\displaystyle=\alpha{\mathbb{E}}_{w\in{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p})}\left[f(x+w)\right]+{\mathbb{E}}_{w\in{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p})}\left[g(x+w)\right]
=α​𝕎σ2​[f]​(x)+𝕎σ2​[g]​(x),\displaystyle=\alpha{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f](x)+{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[g](x)\kern 5.0pt,

which is the result. ∎

Proposition B.3 (𝕎σ2{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}} is increasing).

Let σ>0\sigma>0, the Weierstrass transform is increasing with respect to the function it applies to. Let ff and gg be two functions from ℝp{\mathbb{R}}^{p} to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} such that for any x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, f⁡(x)≤g⁡(x)f(x)\leq g(x), then for any x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p},

𝕎σ2​[f]​(x)≤𝕎σ2​[g]​(x).{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f](x)\leq{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[g](x).
Proof.

By increasing property of the expectation, for a given x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p},

𝕎σ2​[f]​(x)\displaystyle{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[f](x) =𝔼w∈𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip)​[f⁡(x+w)]≤𝔼w∈𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Ip)​[g⁡(x+w)]=𝕎σ2​[g]​(x),\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{w\in{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p})}\left[f(x+w)\right]\leq{\mathbb{E}}_{w\in{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{p})}\left[g(x+w)\right]={\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}[g](x),

and the lemma follows. ∎

We state and prove Remark 3.4.

Proposition B.4 (The exponential loss is in ΦMa,a​(ℝp)\Phi_{M_{a},a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})).

Let f⁡(x)=exp⁡(−θ⊤​x​y)f(x)=\exp(-\theta^{\top}xy) for a given pair (θ,y)∈Θ×𝒴(\theta,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{Y}}. Define Ma=exp⁡(‖Θ‖24​a)M_{a}=\exp\left(\frac{\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}}{4a}\right) for any a>0a>0. The function ff is in ΦMa,a​(ℝp)\Phi_{M_{a},a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p}) for any a>0a>0.

Proof.

We first verify the property of Equation (3). Let an arbitrary a>0a>0. Let k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} and x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, we have the following Laplacian identity

Δxk​f​(x)=|Δxk​f​(x)|=‖θ‖2​k​f​(x).\Delta^{k}_{x}f(x)=|\Delta^{k}_{x}f(x)|=\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2k}f(x).

Factorials are increasing faster than any power of a positive number. Then, denoting k0k_{0} such that for any k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}},

k>k0⟹k!>(‖θ‖/4​a)2​k,k>k_{0}\implies k!>(\left\|{\theta}\right\|/4a)^{2k},

we have

|Δxk​f​(x)|≤Ax​(4​a)k​k!,|\Delta^{k}_{x}f(x)|\leq A_{x}(4a)^{k}k!\kern 5.0pt,

with Ax=f⁡(x)​(‖θ‖2/4​a)k0A_{x}=f(x)(\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}/4a)^{k_{0}}. We now verify that the property of Equation (2) holds with Ma=exp⁡(‖Θ‖24​a)M_{a}=\exp\left(\frac{\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}}{4a}\right). Let x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p},

f⁡(x)=exp⁡(−θ⊤​x​y)≤exp⁡(‖θ‖​‖x‖)≤exp⁡(‖Θ‖​‖x‖).f(x)=\exp(-\theta^{\top}xy)\leq\exp(\|\theta\|\|x\|)\leq\exp(\|\Theta\|\|x\|).

To prove that that exp⁡(‖Θ‖​‖x‖)≤Ma​exp⁡(a​‖x‖2)\exp(\|\Theta\|\|x\|)\leq M_{a}\exp(a\left\|{x}\right\|^{2}), we need that

a​‖x‖2−‖Θ‖​‖x‖+log⁡(Ma)≥0.a\|x\|^{2}-\left\|{\Theta}\right\|\|x\|+\log(M_{a})\geq 0.

It forms a second degree polynomial in ‖x‖\left\|{x}\right\| with a positive quadratic constant. The inequality is then true for any ‖x‖>0\left\|{x}\right\|>0 if the discriminant ‖Θ‖2−4​a​log⁡(Ma)\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}-4a\log(M_{a}) is positive. In other words, if

Ma≤exp⁡(‖Θ‖24​a).M_{a}\leq\exp\left(\frac{\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}}{4a}\right).

Thus, for any a>0a>0, Equation (2) holds with Ma=exp⁡(‖Θ‖24​a)M_{a}=\exp\left(\frac{\left\|{\Theta}\right\|^{2}}{4a}\right), and ff is in ΦMa,a​(ℝp)\Phi_{M_{a},a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p}) for any a>0a>0. ∎

D.1 Inverse of Transforms – Proof of Theorem 5.1

We provide a proof of the following theorem. See 5.1

Proof.

={1}​g​(y~)+{0}​g​(−y~)=g⁡(y~).\displaystyle=\{1\}g(\tilde{y})+\{0\}g(-\tilde{y})=g(\tilde{y}).

Now we prove (ii). We use the parameterization σ2=2​t\sigma^{2}=2t, it remains to reinject σ2\sigma^{2} to finish the proof. By Theorem 3.3 proof, the series t↦∑kΔxk​f​(x)k!​tkt\mapsto\sum_{k}\frac{\Delta_{x}^{k}f(x)}{k!}t^{k} converges absolutely for tt in ]0,1/4​a[]0,1/4a[ for any x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}. Since considering the series for −t-t leads to the same coefficients in absolute value, then the series t↦∑k(−1)k​Δxk​f​(x)k!​tkt\mapsto\sum_{k}\frac{(-1)^{k}\Delta_{x}^{k}f(x)}{k!}t^{k} also converges for 0<t<1/4​a0<t<1/4a.

(𝕎2​t∘𝕎2​t−1)​[f]​(x)\displaystyle({\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\circ{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1})[f](x) =𝕎2​t​[∑j=0∞(−t)jj!​Δj​[f]​(⋅)]​(x)=∑k=0∞tkk!​Δj​[∑k=0∞(−t)jj!​Δj​[f]​(⋅)]​(x).\displaystyle={\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\left[\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{j}}{j!}\Delta^{j}[f](\cdot)\right](x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{k}}{k!}\Delta^{j}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{j}}{j!}\Delta^{j}[f](\cdot)\right](x).

We want to reorder the series and swap ∑k=0∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} with Δj\Delta^{j} to obtain

(𝕎2​t∘𝕎2​t−1)​[f]​(x)=∑j=0∞∑k=0∞(−t)j​tkj!​k!​Δk+j​[f]​(x).({\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\circ{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1})[f](x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{j}t^{k}}{j!k!}\Delta^{k+j}[f](x).

That is valid if the resulting series converges absolutely. This is indeed the case since

∑j=0∞∑k=0∞tj+kj!​k!​|Δk+j​[f]​(x)|\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{j+k}}{j!k!}\left|\Delta^{k+j}[f](x)\right| ≤∑j=0∞∑k=0∞tj+kj!​k!​Ax​(4​a)j+k​(j+k)!\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{j+k}}{j!k!}A_{x}(4a)^{j+k}(j+k)!
↓Reordering (valid by positivity) with n=k+j.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small Reordering (valid by positivity) with $n=k+j$.}}}
=∑n=0∞∑j=0ntn(n−j)!​j!​Ax​(4​a)n​n!\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{t^{n}}{(n-j)!j!}A_{x}(4a)^{n}n!
=Ax​∑n=0∞(4​a​t)n​∑j=0n(nj)\displaystyle=A_{x}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(4at)^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}
↓As ∑j=0n(nj)=2n.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small As $\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}=2^{n}$.}}}
=Ax​∑n=0∞(8​a​t)n\displaystyle=A_{x}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(8at)^{n}
↓As 8​a​t<1.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small As $8at<1$.}}}
=Ax1−8​a​t<∞.\displaystyle=\frac{A_{x}}{1-8at}<\infty.

Then the reordering and swap of derivative and series are valid. We can thus write

(𝕎2​t∘𝕎2​t−1)​[f]​(x)\displaystyle({\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\circ{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1})[f](x) =∑j=0∞∑k=0∞(−t)j​tkj!​k!​Δk+j​[f]​(x)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{j}t^{k}}{j!k!}\Delta^{k+j}[f](x)
↓Same reordering with n=k+j.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small Same reordering with $n=k+j$.}}}
=∑n=0∞∑j=0n(−1)j​tn(n−j)!​j!​Δn​[f]​(x)\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{j}t^{n}}{(n-j)!j!}\Delta^{n}[f](x)
=∑n=0∞tn​Δn​[f]​(x)n!​∑j=0n(nj)​(−1)j​1n−j=∑n=0∞tn​Δn​[f]​(x)n!​(1−1)n\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{n}\Delta^{n}[f](x)}{n!}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}(-1)^{j}1^{n-j}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{n}\Delta^{n}[f](x)}{n!}(1-1)^{n}
=0n​Δ0​[f]​(x)0!\displaystyle=\frac{0^{n}\Delta^{0}[f](x)}{0!}
↓With the convention that 00=1.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small With the convention that $0^{0}=1$.}}}
=f⁡(x).\displaystyle=f(x).

We reparameterize with σ2=2​t\sigma^{2}=2t, then for a<1/4​σ2a<1/4\sigma^{2}, (𝕎σ2∘𝕎σ2−1)​[f]=f({\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}\circ{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1})[f]=f. ∎

D.2 Commutativity of the gradient operator with the transforms

Proposition D.1.

Let ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0, and let ℓ\ell be a loss which satisfies 4.1 with a<1/2​σ2a<1/2\sigma^{2}. Then 𝕋ϵ,δ{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta} and 𝕋ϵ,δ−1{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1} applied to θ↦ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)\theta\mapsto\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot), commute with ∇θ\nabla_{\theta}.

Proof.

Let a tuple (θ,x,y)∈Θ×𝒳×𝒴(\theta,x,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}, we express 𝕋−1{\mathbb{T}}^{-1} with 𝔹−1{\mathbb{B}}^{-1} and 𝕎−1{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}:

∇θ𝕋ϵ,δ−1\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1} [ℓ(θ,⋅,⋅)](x,y)=∇θ[𝔹ϵy−1[z↦𝕎σ2−1[ℓ(θ,⋅,z)](x)](y)]\displaystyle[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](x,y)=\nabla_{\theta}\left[{\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}^{-1}\left[z\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,z)](x)\right](y)\right]
↓Replacing 𝕎−1 with its expression.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small Replacing ${\mathbb{W}}^{-1}$ with its expression.}}}
=∇θ[𝔹ϵy−1[z↦∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!Δxkℓ(θ,x,z)](y)]\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\left[{\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}^{-1}\left[z\mapsto\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,z)\right](y)\right]
↓Replacing 𝔹−1 with its expression.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small Replacing ${\mathbb{B}}^{-1}$ with its expression.}}}
=∇θ[S~​(ϵy)​∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,y)+(1−S~​(ϵy))​∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,−y)]\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\left[\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y)+\left(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\right)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,-y)\right]
↓By linearity of gradients with the finite sum.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small By linearity of gradients with the finite sum.}}}
=S~​(ϵy)​∇θ[∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,y)]+(1−S~​(ϵy))​∇θ[∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,−y)].\displaystyle=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\nabla_{\theta}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y)\right]+\left(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\right)\nabla_{\theta}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,-y)\right]. (12)

We now check for yy and −y-y if we can swap the series and gradients. The reasoning is the same for both and we then present it only for yy. By series differentiation (Rudin, 1976., Theorem 7.17), if the series ∑m=1∞σ2​m2m​m!​|∂θjΔxm​ℓ​(θ,x,y)|\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2m}}{2^{m}m!}|\partial_{\theta_{j}}\Delta^{m}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y)| converges for each component j∈{1,…,k}j\in\{1,\dots,k\}, then

∇θ[∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x,y)]=∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​∇θΔxk​ℓ​(θ,x,y).\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y)\right]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\nabla_{\theta}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y). (13)

As Δk\Delta^{k} is a finite sum of iterated derivatives, it commutes with ∇θ\nabla_{\theta}. We then need to check that for j∈{1,…,k}j\in\{1,\dots,k\},

∑m=0∞σ2​m2m​m!​Δxm​[∂θjℓ⁡(θ,x,y)]\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2m}}{2^{m}m!}\Delta^{m}_{x}\left[\partial_{\theta_{j}}\ell(\theta,x,y)\right]

is a convergent series. By hypothesis on the loss, we have ∂θjℓ⁡(θ,x,y)∈ΦM,a​(ℝp)\partial_{\theta_{j}}\ell(\theta,x,y)\in{\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}, then

∑m=0∞σ2​m2m​m!​|Δxm​[∂θjℓ⁡(θ,x,y)]|≤∑m=0∞σ2​m2m​m!​Ax​(4​a)m=Ax​∑m=0∞(2​a​σ2)m=Ax1−2​a​σ2<∞,\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2m}}{2^{m}m!}\left|\Delta^{m}_{x}\left[\partial_{\theta_{j}}\ell(\theta,x,y)\right]\right|\leq\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\sigma^{2m}}{2^{m}m!}A_{x}(4a)^{m}=A_{x}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(2a\sigma^{2})^{m}=\frac{A_{x}}{1-2a\sigma^{2}}<\infty,

where the last inequality follows from 2​a​σ2<12a\sigma^{2}<1. Injecting Equation 13 in Equation (12) and swapping Δk\Delta^{k} and ∇θ\nabla_{\theta} yields

∇θ𝕋ϵ,δ−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(x,y)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](x,y) =S~​(ϵy)​∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​∇θΔxk​ℓ​(θ,x,y)+(1−S~​(ϵy))​∑k=0∞(−1)k​σ2​k2k​k!​∇θΔxk​ℓ​(θ,x,−y)\displaystyle=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\nabla_{\theta}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,y)+\left(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\right)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}\sigma^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}\nabla_{\theta}\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,x,-y)
=𝔹ϵy−1[z↦𝕎σ2−1[∇θℓ(θ,⋅,z)](x)](y).\displaystyle={\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}^{-1}\left[z\mapsto{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1}[\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,\cdot,z)](x)\right](y).

The exact same reasoning can be carried out with 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} replacing S~\tilde{S} by SS and the terms (−1)k(-1)^{k} by 11 which does not affect the convergence of series involved. ∎

=𝔹ϵy​[𝕎σ2​[𝕎σ2−1​[𝔹ϵ,δ−1​[h⁡(⋅,⋅)]]]]​(x,y)\displaystyle={\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}\left[{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}\left[{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}_{\sigma^{2}}\left[{\mathbb{B}}^{-1}_{\epsilon,\delta}[h(\cdot,\cdot)]\right]\right]\right](x,y)
↓Simplifying 𝕎∘𝕎−1.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small Simplifying ${\mathbb{W}}\circ{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}$.}}}
=𝔹ϵy​[𝔹ϵ,δ−1​[h⁡(⋅,⋅)]]​(x,y)\displaystyle={\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}\left[{\mathbb{B}}^{-1}_{\epsilon,\delta}[h(\cdot,\cdot)]\right](x,y)

↓By commutativity of ∇θ and 𝕋ϵ,δ−1.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small By commutativity of $\nabla_{\theta}$ and ${\mathbb{T}}^{-1}_{\epsilon,\delta}$.}}}
=𝕋ϵ,δ[∇θ𝕋ϵ,δ−1[ℓ(θ,⋅,⋅)](x,y)\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}\left[\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{T}}^{-1}_{\epsilon,\delta}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)\right](x,y)

=∇θ𝕋ϵ,δ[𝕋ϵ,δ−1[ℓ(θ,⋅,⋅)](x,y)\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}\left[{\mathbb{T}}^{-1}_{\epsilon,\delta}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)\right](x,y)

=∇θℓ​(θ,x,y).\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,x,y).

∎

We now have an unbiased estimator of any function f∈ΦM,a​(ℝp)f\in{\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})} at any point x∈ℝpx\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p} from a Gaussian-perturbed release of the point x+wx+w for which we can compute the variance exactly.

The variance can be derived in closed-form for known functions like:

  • •

    if f⁡(x)=12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x+cf(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x+c, then 𝕍w​(𝕎2​t−1​[f]​(x+w))=f2​(x)+2​t​‖Σ​x+b‖2+2​t2​Tr⁡(Σ2){\mathbb{V}}_{w}({\mathbb{W}}^{-1}_{2t}[f](x+w))=f^{2}(x)+2t\left\|{\Sigma x+b}\right\|^{2}+2t^{2}\Tr(\Sigma^{2}) with Σ=(A+A⊤)/2\Sigma=(A+A^{\top})/2,

  • •

    if f⁡(x)=exp⁡(α⊤​x),α∈ℝpf(x)=\exp(\alpha^{\top}x),\;\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, then 𝕍w​(𝕎2​t−1​[f]​(x+w))=exp⁡(2​a⊤​x+2​t​‖a‖2){\mathbb{V}}_{w}({\mathbb{W}}^{-1}_{2t}[f](x+w))=\exp(2a^{\top}x+2t\|a\|^{2}).

Particular cases of the examples are respectively the mean squared error and the exponential loss (see subsection 5.2).

Similarly, the existence of an inverse 𝔹ϵ−1{\mathbb{B}}^{-1}_{\epsilon}, means that for any function g:{−1,1}→ℝg:\{-1,1\}\to{\mathbb{R}}, any y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

C=sup(θ,x,y)∈Θ×𝒳×𝒴,s<σ2/2max⁡{‖∇θℓ​(θ,x,y)‖,‖𝕎2​s−1​[∇θ∇x​ℓ​(θ,⋅,y)]​(x)‖},\displaystyle C=\sup_{(\theta,x,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}},s<\sigma^{2}/2}\max\big\{\left\|{\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,x,y)}\right\|,\left\|{{\mathbb{W}}_{2s}^{-1}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\nabla_{x}\ell(\theta,\cdot,y)\right](x)}\right\|\big\},

D.5 Application to Generalized Linear Models (GLM)

We provide proofs of derivations for the case of GLM (subsection 5.2).

Loss.

Recall that in GLM the loss is ℓ⁡(θ,x~,y~)=f⁡(θ⊤​x~​y~)\ell(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})=f(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}). It simplifies the expression of iterated Laplacians:

Δxk​f​(θ⊤​x~​y~)=‖θ‖2​k​f(2​k)​(θ⊤​x~​y~).\Delta^{k}_{x}f(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y})=\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2k}f^{(2k)}(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y})\kern 5.0pt.

Then, the Weierstrass inverse has the following expression.

𝕎2​t−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,y~)]​(x~)\displaystyle{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\tilde{y})](\tilde{x}) =∑k=0∞Δxk​ℓ​(θ,x~,y~)k!​(−t)k=∑k=0∞Δxk​f​(θ⊤​x~​y~)k!​(−t)k\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Delta^{k}_{x}\ell(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}{k!}(-t)^{k}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Delta^{k}_{x}f(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y})}{k!}(-t)^{k}

Recall Equation (6):

ℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)\displaystyle\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) =𝕋ϵ,δ−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(x~,y~)=𝕎σ2−1​[𝔹ϵy​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(⋅,y~)]​(x~)\displaystyle={\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](\tilde{x},\tilde{y})={\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1}\left[{\mathbb{B}}_{\epsilon_{y}}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](\cdot,\tilde{y})\right](\tilde{x})

=S~​(ϵy)​𝕎σ2−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,y~)]​(x~)+(1−S~​(ϵy))​𝕎σ2−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,−y~)]​(x~).\displaystyle=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y}){\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\tilde{y})](\tilde{x})+\left(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\right){\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,-\tilde{y})](\tilde{x})\kern 5.0pt.

ℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)=S~​(ϵy)​𝕎σ2​‖θ‖2−1​[f]​(θ⊤​x~​y~)+(1−S~​(ϵy))​𝕎σ2​‖θ‖2−1​[f]​(−θ⊤​x~​y~).\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y}){\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}}^{-1}[f]\left(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\right)+\left(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\right){\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}}^{-1}[f]\left(-\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\right).

Gradient.

We can’t directly differentiate Equation (6) with respect to θ\theta by swaping Weierstrass transform and gradient (∇θ𝕎2​t−1​[ℓ⁡(θ,⋅,y~)]=𝕎2​t−1​[∇θℓ​(θ,⋅,y~)]\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[\ell(\theta,\cdot,\tilde{y})]={\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,\cdot,\tilde{y})]) because here tt depends on θ\theta. ∇θℓ~ϵ,δ​(θ,x~,y~)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\tilde{\ell}_{\epsilon,\delta}(\theta,\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) =S~​(ϵy)​∇θ𝕎σ2​‖θ‖2−1​[f]​(θ⊤​x~​y~)+(1−S~​(ϵy))​∇θ𝕎σ2​‖θ‖2−1​[f]​(−θ⊤​x~​y~).\displaystyle=\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}}^{-1}[f]\left(\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\right)+\left(1-\tilde{S}(\epsilon_{y})\right)\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{W}}_{\sigma^{2}\left\|{\theta}\right\|^{2}}^{-1}[f]\left(-\theta^{\top}\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\right).

D.7 In Absence of Closed-form Expression for 𝕎−1{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}

When no closed-form expression of 𝕎−1​[f]{\mathbb{W}}^{-1}[f] is given, we fall into two cases

  1. 1.

    ff is in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})},

  2. 2.

    ff is not in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}.

In the two cases, we use the following approximation of 𝕎2​t−1​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[f]:

gtK​(x)=∑k=0KΔk​f​(x)k!​(−t)k.g^{K}_{t}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{\Delta^{k}f(x)}{k!}(-t)^{k}.

In case 1 (ff is in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}), we can bound the bias of gtKg^{K}_{t} uniformly on 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} using the fact that limK→∞gtK​(x)=𝕎2​t−1​[f]​(x)\lim_{K\to\infty}g^{K}_{t}(x)={\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[f](x),

biasK\displaystyle\text{bias}_{K} =supx∈𝒳|𝕎2​t​[gtK]​(x)−f⁡(x)|=supx∈𝒳|𝕎2​t​[gtK−𝕎2​t−1​[f]]​(x)|\displaystyle=\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}|{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\left[g^{K}_{t}\right](x)-f(x)|=\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left|{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\left[g^{K}_{t}-{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[f]\right](x)\right|
≤supx∈𝒳|gtK​(x)−𝕎2​t−1​[f]​(x)|=supx∈𝒳|∑k=K+1∞Δk​f​(x)k!​(−t)k|\displaystyle\leq\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left|g^{K}_{t}(x)-{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[f](x)\right|=\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left|\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}\frac{\Delta^{k}f(x)}{k!}(-t)^{k}\right|
↓By Equation (3), it exist D>0 such that\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\,~\downarrow{}\;{\text{\small By Equation~\eqref{eq:laplace_iterate_growth}, it exist $D>0$ such that}}}
≤D​supx∈𝒳Ax​(4​a​t)K+1.\displaystyle\leq D\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}A_{x}(4at)^{K+1}.

Then, the bias of using gtKg^{K}_{t} instead of 𝕎2​t−1​[f]{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}^{-1}[f] is exponentially decreasing with KK since a<1/4​ta<1/4t.
In case 2 (ff is not in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}), we do not have any guarantee that increasing KK will result in a better approximation. Instead, we can estimate the b​i​a​sKbias_{K} for small K∈{1,2,3,…}K\in\{1,2,3,\dots\} and take the optimal truncation (Boyd, 1999):

K∗\displaystyle K^{*} =argminK{biasK=supx∈𝒳|𝕎2​t[gtK](x)−f(x)|}\displaystyle=\arg\min_{K}\left\{bias_{K}=\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left|{\mathbb{W}}_{2t}\left[g^{K}_{t}\right](x)-f(x)\right|\right\}
=arg⁡minK​{supx∈𝒳|∫0t(−s)KK!​𝕎2​s​[ΔK+1​f]​(x)​𝑑s|}.\displaystyle=\arg\min_{K}\left\{\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left|\int_{0}^{t}\frac{(-s)^{K}}{K!}{\mathbb{W}}_{2s}\left[\Delta^{K+1}f\right](x)ds\right|\right\}\kern 5.0pt.

We present this case for the example of the log loss.

Example 4 (log loss).

Consider f⁡(θ⊤​x​y)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−θ⊤​x​y))f\left(\theta^{\top}xy\right)=\log(1+\exp(-\theta^{\top}xy)) for any (θ,x,y)∈Θ×𝒳×𝒴(\theta,x,y)\in\Theta\times{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}. ff is not in ΦM,a​(ℝp){\Phi_{M,a}({\mathbb{R}}^{p})}. Figure 3 shows the estimate of the truncation error εK\varepsilon_{K} via numerical integration and Monte-Carlo sampling approximation. We restrict the study to t≤25t\leq 25 which, for the unit ball ‖𝒳‖≤1\left\|{{\mathcal{X}}}\right\|\leq 1, is true for any ϵ≥1\epsilon\geq 1. For low tt, choosing K∈{2,3}K\in\{2,3\} can be better and for larger one K=1K=1 is showing a smaller bias.

D.8 Convergence of IWP-SGD – Proof of Theorem 5.5

We provide a proof of the following theorem. See 5.5

Proof.

First, the algorithm is (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP by the post-processing theorem as the data is first privatized using the (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP release (1) before being used for the SGD iterations. The rest of the proof is about the convergence guarantees. For any t≥0t\geq 0 the iterates of SGD are given by:

θt+1=ΠΘ​(θt−γ​gt),\displaystyle\theta_{t+1}=\Pi_{\Theta}(\theta_{t}-\gamma g_{t}), (18)

where γ>0\gamma>0 denotes a step-size and gtg_{t} is the IWP gradient estimator computed on the (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP release defined in Equation (1)

gt=𝕋ϵ,δ−1​[∇θℓ​(θ,⋅,⋅)]​(x~,y~).g_{t}={\mathbb{T}}_{\epsilon,\delta}^{-1}[\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,\cdot,\cdot)](\tilde{x},\tilde{y}).

For any t≥0t\geq 0, the expectation of gtg_{t} is

𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝔼(x~,y~)[gt∣θ0,…,θt]=∇ℛ(θt),\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[g_{t}\mid\theta_{0},\dots,\theta_{t}\right]=\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\theta_{t}), (19)

and the squared gradient satisfies

𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝔼(x~,y~)[∥gt∥2∣θ0,…,θt]=‖∇ℛ(θt)‖2+𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝔼(x~,y~)[‖gt−∇ℛ(θt)‖2∣θ0,…,θt].\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}\left[\|g_{t}\|^{2}\mid\theta_{0},\dots,\theta_{t}\right]=\left\|{\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\theta_{t})}\right\|^{2}+{\mathbb{E}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})}[\left\|{g_{t}-\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\theta_{t})}\right\|^{2}\mid\theta_{0},\dots,\theta_{t}]\kern 5.0pt.

Let t≥0t\geq 0. Then

where we also used μ\mu-strong convexity in the last inequality. By re-arranging and taking expectation on both sides, we get:

and by observing (1−𝒦​γ)≥12(1-{\mathcal{K}}\gamma)\geq\frac{1}{2} for γ≤12​𝒦\gamma\leq\frac{1}{2{\mathcal{K}}},

This intermediate results shows that SGD with constant stepsizes reduces the initial error term ‖θ0−θ⋆‖2\left\|{\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}}\right\|^{2} linearly, but only converges towards a 𝒪⁡(γμ​C2​eϵy(eϵy−1)2​(σ2+1)){\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\gamma}{\mu}\frac{C^{2}e^{\epsilon_{y}}}{(e^{\epsilon_{y}}-1)^{2}}(\sigma^{2}+1)\right)-neighborhood of θ⋆\theta^{\star}.

Choosing the Step-size.

To obtain a convergence guarantee that holds for arbitrary accuracy, we need to choose the stepsize γ\gamma carefully:

  • •

    If 12​𝒦≥1μ​n​log⁡max⁡(2,μ2​‖θ0−θ⋆‖2​nA)\frac{1}{2{\mathcal{K}}}\geq\frac{1}{\mu n}\log\max\left(2,\frac{\mu^{2}\left\|{\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}}\right\|^{2}n}{A}\right) then we choose γ=1μ​n​log⁡max⁡(2,μ2​‖θ0−θ⋆‖2​nA)\gamma=\frac{1}{\mu n}\log\max\left(2,\frac{\mu^{2}\left\|{\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}}\right\|^{2}n}{A}\right).

  • •

    If otherwise 12​𝒦<1μ​n​log⁡max⁡(2,μ2​‖θ0−θ⋆‖2​nA)\frac{1}{2{\mathcal{K}}}<\frac{1}{\mu n}\log\max\left(2,\frac{\mu^{2}\left\|{\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}}\right\|^{2}n}{A}\right) then we pick γ=12​𝒦\gamma=\frac{1}{2{\mathcal{K}}}.
